blocks.text: Across Central New York, West Virginia, and Pennsylvania, towns and rural communities bear the marks of industries that once promised prosperity. Coal mines, factories, agriculture, and power plants shaped the land and provided generations of work. As industries declined, consolidated, or disappeared, they left behind altered landscapes, shrinking towns, economic hardship, and communities searching for what comes next.

Aftermath Country examines life within this prolonged transition. Abandoned buildings and industrial remnants exist alongside homes, farms, businesses, and new infrastructure. Poverty and decline are visible, but so are persistence and attempts at revival. People continue to build lives in places too often understood only through what they have lost.

Now, another transformation is beginning. Renewable energy, revived power plants, and the rapid expansion of data centers are bringing new investment and new demands for land and electricity to some of these same regions. They carry another promise of economic renewal, while raising familiar questions about who benefits, who leaves, and what will remain afterward.

The project looks at the cycle of prosperity, decline, and reinvention that has repeatedly shaped these communities. It asks what “revival” means in places still living with the consequences of previous transformations, and whether the arrival of something new can ever be separated from what came before.
